en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section The Second Chapter
Regarding the discussion on vocal expression:
Is there vocal expression for one who has entered meditative absorption? Yes.

If you say that for those who have attained meditative absorption there is vocal expression, you should not speak thus … [as before] … Do you maintain that for one who has attained absorption there is vocal expression? Yes.
Is there vocal expression for those who have attained meditative absorption at all times?
One should not say so... [etc. ...
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained meditative absorption?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Is there vocal expression for all those who have attained meditative absorption?
“One should not say so,” … [and so on].
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained meditative absorption?
Yes. Is there vocal expression in all meditative absorptions?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is there vocal expression for one who has attained meditative absorption? Yes.
Is there bodily dissolution for one who has attained meditative absorption?
One should not say so …pe… Is there no bodily dissolution for one who has attained meditative absorption?
“Yes.
“Then for one who has attained [meditative absorption], there is no vocal expression?
“One should not say so” …pe…
Is there speech for one who has attained meditative absorption? Is there a vocal differentiation for one who has attained meditative absorption? Yes.
Is there a body for one who has attained meditative absorption? Is there a bodily differentiation for one who has attained meditative absorption?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … For one who has attained [meditative absorption], does the body exist, but the breaking up of the body does not exist? Yes.
Does one who has attained [meditative absorption] possess speech, yet there is no vocal utterance?
One should not say so...pe...
Does one who knows "it is suffering" utter the words "it is suffering"?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Does one who knows ‘this is arising’ utter the speech, ‘This is arising’?
“One should not say so,” … [and so on] …
If one knows "it is suffering," does one utter the words "it is suffering"?
Yes. If one knows "it is cessation," does one utter the words "it is cessation"? Yes.
It should not be said thus... [etc.
...Is it the case that one who knows "it is suffering" utters the words "it is suffering"? Yes.
If one knows it is a "maggot," does one speak the word "maggot"?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...If one knows it is an "origination" (samudaya), does one not speak the word "origination"?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Does one who knows ‘it is suffering’ not speak the words ‘it is not suffering’? [The respondent replies:
“One should certainly not say that …” and so forth.
One who knows "this is cessation" does not speak the words "this is not cessation," does one? Yes.
One who knows "this is suffering" does not speak the words "this is not suffering," does one?
It should not be said thus...
[as before] ...Is it the case that one who knows "this is the path" does not utter the words "this is not the path"? Yes.
"One who knows 'this is suffering' does not utter the words 'this is not suffering,' is that so?
"One should not say so. ... [etc.
... "Does one who has attained meditative absorption possess vocal expression?"
“Yes.
“What is the range of knowledge?
“The range of knowledge is the truths.”
Is the ear the domain of truth?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Does one who has attained meditative absorption have vocal expression?
“Yes.
“What is the objective domain of the ear?
“The ear has sound as its objective domain.”
Is knowledge whose objective domain is sound?
One should not say so.
Does one who has attained meditative absorption have vocal expression? Knowledge has truth as its objective domain; the ear has sound as its objective domain. Is this so?
“Yes,” [you say].
But if knowledge has the truths as its domain and the ear has sounds as its domain, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
“For one who has attained meditative absorption, there is vocal expression.”
For one who has attained [jhāna], is there vocal expression, and is there knowledge whose domain is the truths, and is there hearing whose domain is sound? Yes.
Is there then a convergence of two types of contact, two types of feeling, two types of perception, two types of volition, and two types of consciousness?
It should not be said so.
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained [meditative absorption]? Yes.
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained the earth-kasina absorption?
One should not say so.
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained [absorption]?
“Yes.
“The water-kasiṇa … the fire-kasiṇa …” [and so forth].
the air kasiṇa … the blue kasiṇa … the yellow kasiṇa …
the red kasiṇa … the white kasiṇa … the base of infinite space …
Is there vocal utterance for one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness … the base of nothingness … the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … When one has attained the earth-kasiṇa attainment, is there no vocal utterance? Yes.
If there is no vocal expression for one who has attained the earth-kasina absorption, then indeed it should not be said that "there is vocal expression for one who has attained.
[The same applies to] the water-kasina ...
the fire-kasina ...
the air kasiṇa … the blue kasiṇa … the yellow kasiṇa …
the red kasiṇa … the white kasiṇa … the base of infinite space …
Is there no vocal expression for one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, or the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
“Yes.
“If there is no vocal expression for one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘There is vocal expression for one who has attained [meditative absorption].’”
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained meditative absorption? Yes.
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained a mundane meditative absorption?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is there vocal expression for one who has attained meditative absorption? Yes.
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained the first mundane jhāna?
One should not say so … [as before] … Is there vocal expression for one who has attained [jhāna]?
“Yes, [it is].
The second mundane jhāna … the third jhāna … [is likewise].
Is there vocal utterance for one who has attained the fourth jhāna?
You should not say so… [as before] … Is there no vocal utterance for one who has attained a mundane attainment?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “If there is no vocal expression for one who has attained a mundane attainment, then indeed, sir, you should not say:
‘There is vocal expression for one who has attained.’”
Is it not the case that for one who has attained the first mundane jhāna, there is no vocal expression?
Yes, it is so.
If, indeed, for one who has attained the first mundane jhāna there is no vocal expression, then surely, sir, you should not say: [that such a person can utter words].
“There is vocal expression for one who has attained [meditative absorption].
This refers to the second worldly jhāna … the third jhāna …
Is it not the case that for one who has attained the fourth jhāna there is no vocal utterance?
Yes, it is so.
If there is indeed no vocal utterance for one who has attained the mundane fourth jhāna, then surely you should not say, "For one who has attained [jhāna], there is vocal utterance."
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained the first supramundane jhāna? Yes.
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained the first mundane jhāna?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is there vocal expression for one who has attained the first supramundane jhāna? Yes.
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained the second worldly jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is it not the case that for one who has attained the first mundane jhāna there is no vocal expression?
Yes, it is.
Is there no vocal utterance for one who has attained the first supramundane jhāna?
One should not say so …pe… [the same applies to] the second mundane jhāna …pe…
Is it not the case that for one who has attained the third jhāna … or the fourth jhāna, there is no utterance of speech?
Yes, it is.
Is it not the case that for one who has attained the first supramundane jhāna, there is no vocal expression?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Is it the case that for one who has attained the first supramundane jhāna, there is vocal expression?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is there vocal utterance for one who has attained the second supramundane jhāna?
You should not say so… [and so on].
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained the first supramundane jhāna? Yes. Is there [vocal expression] for one who has attained the third supramundane jhāna? ...
Is there vocal expression for one who has attained the fourth jhāna?
One should not say so… [as before] … Is there no vocal expression for one who has attained the supramundane second jhāna?
“Yes.
“For one who has attained the first supramundane jhāna, there is no vocal expression?
“One must not say so … [and so on].”
Is there no vocal expression for one who has attained the second supramundane jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna?
“Yes,” [you say].
“But for one who has attained the first supramundane jhāna, there is no vocal expression?
You should not say so … [and so on] … No, you should not say that.
Is it not to be said that for one who has attained meditative absorption there is vocal expression?
Yes, it is.
But has it not been said by the Blessed One that initial application and sustained application are verbal formations—
"For one who has attained the first jhāna, there is initial application and sustained application"?
Yes, it has.
If it is said by the Blessed One that applied thought and sustained thought are verbal formations—
"For one who has attained the first jhāna, there is applied thought and sustained thought"— then, indeed, it must be said of him:
"There is vocal utterance for one who has attained."
The Blessed One has stated that initial application and sustained application are verbal formations:
"For one who has attained the first jhāna, there is initial application and sustained application. Does it follow, therefore, that there is vocal expression for such a person?
Yes, it does.
"For one who has attained the first jhāna through the earth-kasiṇa, there are applied thought and sustained thought; does he have vocal expression?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...Applied thought and sustained thought have been called "verbal formations" by the Blessed One.

“If one who has attained the first jhāna possesses applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), does he possess vocal expression?”— “Yes.”— “Does one who has attained the water-kasiṇa [possess vocal expression]?”— “Yes.”
the fire kasiṇa … the air kasiṇa … the blue kasiṇa …
For one who has attained the first jhāna with the yellow kasiṇa … the red kasiṇa … or the white kasiṇa, are there applied thought and sustained thought, and is there vocal expression for him?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Should it not be said that “for one who has attained meditative absorption, there is vocal expression”?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Is it not stated by the Blessed One that speech is originated by applied thought:
‘For one who has attained the first jhāna, there are applied thought and sustained thought’?”
“Yes.

[The opponent asks: “If it is true that speech originated by applied thought was spoken by the Blessed One when he said, ‘For one who has attained the first jhāna, there are applied thought and sustained thought,’ then indeed, sir, you must say this:”
“Does one who has attained [jhāna] have vocal expression?
Speech was described by the Blessed One as being originated by applied thought:
“For one who has attained the first jhāna, there are applied thought and sustained thought. Does that person have vocal expression?
“Yes.
“Speech has been described by the Blessed One as originating from perception.
Does one who has attained the second jhāna have perception? And does he still have applied thought and sustained thought?”
It should not be said so… [as before]… Speech is said by the Blessed One to be originated by thought:
“For one who has attained the first jhāna, there are applied thought and sustained thought. Does it follow that for such a person there is vocal expression?
“Yes.
“Speech has been described by the Blessed One as originating from perception:
‘The third jhāna…’” [and so on].
the fourth jhāna … the base of infinite space … the base of infinite consciousness …
Is there perception for one who has attained the base of nothingness? Is there applied thought and sustained thought for him?
One should not say so… [and so on]… Is there vocal expression for one who has attained it?
“Yes,” he says.
“Is it not true that ‘for one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has ceased’?
Is there not such a sutta?”
“Yes.
“If it is true that ‘for one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has ceased,’ then this Sutta passage indeed exists; yet, O friend, you must not say:
‘For one who has attained [jhāna], there is vocal expression.’”
“If it is true that ‘for one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has ceased,’ as this is indeed a sutta, does that person still possess vocal expression?”— Yes.

“If it is true that ‘for one who has attained the second jhāna, applied thought and sustained thought have ceased,’ as this is indeed a sutta, does that person still possess applied thought and sustained thought?”— No.
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … If it is true that there is a sutta stating,
“For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has ceased,” does that person still possess vocal activity? Yes.
“For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has ceased; for one who has attained the fourth jhāna, inhalation and exhalation have ceased;

for one who has attained the base of infinite space, the perception of form has ceased; for one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space has ceased;
for one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness [has ceased].”
"If it is said: 'For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness has ceased;
for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, both perception and feeling have ceased'—is this a sutta that exists?
And if so, does he still possess perception and feeling?"
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Should it not be said:
“For one who has attained meditative absorption, there is vocal expression”?
“Yes. [The opponent asks:
“Is it not true that ‘sound was called a thorn to the first jhāna by the Blessed One’?”
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “If sound is called a ‘thorn’ for the first jhāna by the Blessed One, then indeed, sir, you must say:
‘For one who has attained [jhāna], there is vocal utterance.’”
It has been said by the Blessed One that sound is a thorn to the first jhāna. Does one who has attained [the first jhāna] still possess vocal expression?
Yes. It has been said by the Blessed One that applied thought and sustained thought are a thorn to the second jhāna...
The Blessed One has said that rapture is a thorn to the third jhāna;
the Blessed One has said that inhalation and exhalation are a thorn to the fourth jhāna;
the Blessed One has said that the perception of form is a thorn for one who has attained the base of infinite space.
For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space is called a "thorn" by the Blessed One;
for one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness is called a "thorn" by the Blessed One;
for one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness is called a "thorn" by the Blessed One.

"Is it not to be said that for one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have been called 'thorns' by the Blessed One, yet perception and feeling still exist in him?
"It is not to be said thus... [and so on].
It is not to be said—
“Does one who has attained [jhāna] have vocal expression?”—
Yes. But was it not said by the Blessed One:

“Ānanda, while standing in the Brahma-world, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had a disciple named Abhibhū who made himself heard by his voice throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system, saying:
‘Exert yourselves! Strive! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!’”
Shake off the army of Death,
as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket—
you who, in this Dhamma and Discipline...
“He will dwell with diligence;
having abandoned the wandering through births,
he will make an end of suffering.”
Is that indeed the Sutta? Yes.
In that case, there is vocal expression for one who has attained meditative absorption.
The Discussion on the Differentiation of Speech is finished.
